sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Strategic Context**: The Marathas aimed to establish 'Hindu Pad Padshahi' across India, clashing with the **Durrani Empire** (Afghan) over control of Delhi and Punjab.
• **Leadership**: Maratha forces were led by **Sadashivrao Bhau** (Peshwa's cousin) and **Vishwasrao** (Peshwa's son), while the Afghan side was led by **Ahmad Shah Abdali**.
• **Alliances**: Abdali secured the support of **Shuja-ud-Daula** (Nawab of Awadh) and **Najib-ud-Daulah** (Rohilla chief), isolating the Marathas.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: The battle was a war of attrition; the Marathas suffered from severe supply chain failures and lack of local support in the Doab region.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix

Mains: Analysis of Maratha failure in 'All-India' diplomacy.
Superior use of light cavalry, swivel guns (Zamburaks), and strategic blockade.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Diplomatic Failure**: Marathas failed to secure the neutrality of the Sikhs and the support of the Rajputs, leading to their isolation.
• **Logistical Collapse**: The Maratha camp was burdened by thousands of non-combatant pilgrims, making them vulnerable to starvation.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Lack of a unified national vision among Indian states.
• **Solutions**: Historical analysis emphasizes the need for 'Realpolitik' over expansionist military adventurism.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'A-S-N' (Abdali, Shuja, Najib).
• **Decoded Meaning**: The three key pillars of the Afghan-led coalition that defeated the Marathas.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often asks if the battle ended the Maratha Empire. It did not; it only checked their expansion, and they recovered under Madhavrao I within a decade.
Mains Value Addition: Quote Sir Jadunath Sarkar: 'The battle decided not who was to rule India, but who was not to rule India.'

keyTakeaways: The battle was a tactical defeat for the Marathas due to poor logistics and diplomatic isolation.
It did not destroy the Maratha Empire but halted their northward expansion.
The primary beneficiary of the battle was the British East India Company, which faced no major challenger in the subsequent decades.
